rewrites.title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-pattern titration
rewrites.description: Drive FOS/JUN activity with an optogenetic or chemically gated system, varying pulse duration, frequency and amplitude while keeping total dose fixed. Then measure persistent chromatin accessibility and response to re-challenge to determine which temporal patterns (e.g., sustained versus pulsatile, as in ERK-to-FOS decoding) establish memory, and whether there is a threshold or bistable switch.

rewrites.title: Single-cell lineage-tracked inheritance across divisions
rewrites.description: Label sister cells with barcodes or time-lapse lineage tracing, with an endogenous AP-1 reporter, and compare memory strength (recall response) among sisters and cousins over several divisions. Heritable correlation beyond what is explained by AP-1 levels would indicate mitotic transmission, and mitotic-chromatin imaging or CUT&Tag of mitotic cells would test mitotic bookmarking.

rewrites.title: Hysteresis measurement with up and down dose ramps
rewrites.description: Ramp the dose of a stimulus (e.g., TPA or growth factor) up and then down in cells, and quantify AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy, chromatin accessibility and target transcription at matched doses. A path-dependent loop, where the same dose gives different outputs on the way up and down, would show that AP-1 retains a memory of past input.

rewrites.title: Time-resolved degron: priming-only vs maintenance-only vs recall-only depletion
rewrites.description: Use an acute auxin/dTAG degron on endogenous AP-1 factors and deplete them only during the priming window, only during the maintenance interval, or only at recall. Memory that requires AP-1 for establishment but not maintenance, or for both, distinguishes a trigger mechanism from a self-sustaining memory mechanism.

rewrites.title: Chromatin residence time of AP-1 after stimulus removal
rewrites.description: Use HaloTag-labeled JUN or FOS with live-cell FRAP or single-molecule tracking to measure how long AP-1 remains bound to chromatin after stimulus withdrawal and how that residence time changes over days. A residence time that stays elevated after the signal ends would provide a binding-level readout of memory.

rewrites.title: Change in AP-1 heterodimer composition as a stored state
rewrites.description: Use endogenous HaloTag or degron knock-ins with proximity ligation to track which Fos-family and Jun-family partners (e.g., c-Fos vs. Fra1, JunB vs. c-Jun, ATF3) form dimers at target sites across stimulation and washout. Test whether a persistent shift in partner ratio, rather than AP-1 presence, predicts faster re-induction, then fix a specific dimer using a fusion construct to see if memory changes.

rewrites.title: Reading AP-1 imprints from sequential stimulation histories
rewrites.description: Use single-cell multiome (scATAC plus RNA) with footprinting or motif-deviation analysis on sequential stimulation histories, such as stimulus A then B, to identify AP-1 imprints from each stimulus. Test whether sites opened by the first stimulus (AP-1-dependent) are distinguishable from sites opened by the second, and whether AP-1 subunit composition (FOS vs JUN vs ATF) encodes the identity of the earlier stimulus.

rewrites.title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-and-removal memory test
rewrites.description: Use an optogenetically controlled c-Jun/c-Fos (or degron-tagged) system to deliver a transient AP-1 pulse, then rapidly remove it and track chromatin accessibility and target gene expression for weeks across cell divisions. Memory is supported only if the accessible state and transcription persist after AP-1 is gone, and it is refuted if they decay with the half-life of AP-1 itself.

rewrites.title: Pulse-frequency dependence of AP-1 memory
rewrites.description: Deliver the same total stimulus dose in microfluidic chambers as a single pulse, several spaced pulses, or continuous exposure, then measure the strength and persistence of the priming signature at a fixed later time. Whether memory scales with integrated dose, the number of pulses, or the timing of the last pulse distinguishes cumulative memory from a reporter of only the most recent event.

rewrites.title: Accumulation of subthreshold repeated stimuli
rewrites.description: Give cells repeated stimulus pulses that are each too weak to trigger a response, at different spacings. Test whether AP-1 occupancy and accessibility build up stepwise until the cells reach a persistent state, and whether the summed AP-1 signal predicts when the switch occurs. This would show AP-1 integrating and storing past exposure.

rewrites.title: dCas9-tethered AP-1 sufficiency test at silent loci
rewrites.description: Tether c-Jun or a p300-recruiting AP-1 fragment to silent loci with dCas9, then wash out and measure whether the locus keeps an open, primed state and responds faster on re-stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 recruitment alone can install memory, independent of upstream signaling.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 depletion after priming to test maintenance versus initiation
rewrites.description: Prime cells with a stimulus such as injury, inflammation or stress, then rapidly degrade all AP-1 (dTAG or dominant-negative A-Fos) at varying delays and measure whether the primed accessibility and faster re-induction persist. If memory persists without AP-1, AP-1 is only an initiator and other factors maintain it. If it is lost, AP-1 is required for maintenance.

rewrites.title: Tethered AP-1 at a silent non-enhancer locus
rewrites.description: Use a dCas9 or zinc-finger tether to recruit c-Jun/Fos to a transcriptionally silent, non-AP-1 locus for a single transient pulse, then track H3K27ac and transcription for weeks. Persistence there, independent of native enhancer context, would show that AP-1 itself establishes a durable state rather than only reading a pre-existing one.

rewrites.title: Sufficiency by synthetic AP-1 induction, with motif editing and in vivo validation
rewrites.description: Optogenetically or chemically drive AP-1 transiently in naive cells and test whether this alone produces lasting accessibility and primed responses. Complement this with CRISPR deletion or mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers (or dCas9 epigenetic editing) to test necessity, and with in vivo validation in a model such as skin epithelial wound memory or trained immunity.

rewrites.title: Acute degron depletion after memory is established
rewrites.description: Make a degron (dTAG or AID) knock-in of a key AP-1 subunit, or express a dominant-negative such as A-FOS. Remove AP-1 only after stimulation has ended and test whether the primed accessibility and the faster re-induction on second challenge are lost. If AP-1 is needed to maintain memory, depletion should erase it. If it is needed only to establish it, the memory should persist.

rewrites.title: Causal closing and opening of retained AP-1 sites
rewrites.description: Use dCas9-KRAB/DNMT3A to selectively close the retained AP-1 enhancers identified previously, and dCas9-p300 or synthetic AP-1 tethering to open them in naive cells, then repeat the graded re-stimulation assay. If these elements carry the memory, closing them should abolish the threshold shift and opening them should produce a primed response in cells never exposed to the stimulus.

rewrites.title: Separating establishment from maintenance with acute AP-1 degradation
rewrites.description: Establish a primed state with a defined stimulus, then use dTAG or auxin degrons to acutely deplete JUN/FOS family proteins only after the stimulus is withdrawn, and ask whether the accessible enhancers, enhancer-promoter contacts, and faster re-induction persist. If memory persists without AP-1 protein, AP-1 establishes a chromatin mark rather than being the memory itself; if memory collapses, AP-1 is continuously required.

rewrites.title: Hysteresis and bistability mapping of the AP-1 dose response
rewrites.description: Expose cells to a graded series of stimulus doses approached from below and from above (stepping up from zero versus stepping down from saturating stimulus) and measure single-cell AP-1 activity at matched steady-state doses. Overlapping curves indicate passive relay of the signal; a hysteresis loop with a bistable regime would show AP-1 is wired as a self-sustaining memory switch, and mutating AP-1 motifs in FOS/JUN's own regulatory elements should abolish the loop.

rewrites.title: Paralog composition switching by time-resolved CUT&RUN and proteomics
rewrites.description: Track which AP-1 dimers occupy memory sites across early, intermediate and late time points using paralog-specific CUT&RUN and BioID/mass spectrometry. If the AP-1 paralog identity or partner transcription factors (e.g., ATF3, BATF, TEAD) shift while accessibility is maintained, memory reflects a handoff rather than persistent AP-1 binding, which discriminates between models.

rewrites.title: Predictive modeling of response from AP-1 state after prior exposure
rewrites.description: Expose isogenic cells to combinations of stimuli separated by defined intervals and fit a model in which the AP-1 state measured after the first exposure predicts the quantitative response to the second, at single-cell resolution. A genuine memory mechanism should make AP-1 state a better predictor of future behavior than current signaling activity or overall cell state, and the model's failures identify additional components that memory requires.
